## Workforce Snapshot: Key Insights

**What stands out:** Active headcount is 1,292 with 13.9% attrition (208 terminations) and only 70 external hires—a significant net workforce contraction. IT (18.3%) and Marketing (17.1%) face the highest attrition, while Engineering (8.1%) and Finance (9.7%) retain talent most effectively.

### Attrition Hot Spots

| Department | Headcount | Terminations | Attrition % |
|------------|-----------|--------------|-------------|
| IT | 94 | 21 | 18.3% |
| Marketing | 102 | 21 | 17.1% |
| Legal | 122 | 24 | 16.4% |
| Engineering | 114 | 10 | 8.1% |
| Finance | 121 | 13 | 9.7% |

**Why this matters:** The top termination reason is "Voluntary - Better Opportunity" (43 cases), signaling competitive pull. With 62 open requisitions and a 71-day average time-to-fill, you're losing talent faster than you can replace it. Gender pay equity is reasonable (Female: $116,630 vs. Male: $116,907), but non-binary employees earn notably less ($105,149). Learning engagement is modest (60.6% completion), and while 307 high potentials exist, retention in high-attrition departments risks losing them.

### Recommended Actions

1. **Retention deep-dive in IT & Marketing:** Conduct exit interviews and stay conversations to identify specific pain points (compensation, career paths, workload). Benchmark pay and advancement opportunities against market.

2. **Accelerate hiring in critical roles:** Partner Recruiting with IT/Marketing hiring managers to reduce time-to-fill; consider referral bonuses and talent pipelines from competitors.

3. **Address non-binary pay equity:** Audit role distribution and salary bands for non-binary employees to close the $11K gap and ensure equitable leveling.

4. **Leverage Engineering/Finance retention practices:** Document what's working in low-attrition departments (mentorship, flexibility, recognition) and replicate enterprise-wide.

# Workforce Overview Analysis

**What stands out:** Your active headcount is 1,292 with an attrition rate of 13.9% (208 terminations), but external hiring has been notably low at only 70 new hires, creating a significant deficit that's shrinking your workforce.

## Key Observations

| Metric | Value | Insight |
|--------|-------|---------|
| **Active Headcount** | 1,292 | Relatively balanced across departments (90-128 per dept) |
| **Terminations** | 208 | 13.9% attrition rate |
| **External Hires** | 70 | Replacing only 34% of exits |
| **Net Change** | -138 | Workforce contracted substantially |
| **Gender Split** | 44.3% Female | Reasonable balance (573F, 655M, 64 Non-binary) |
| **Generational** | 43% Millennial | Healthy age diversity with 241 Gen Z |

The hire/termination data shows consistent attrition from tenure cohorts (2011-2024 hires) with 208 total exits, while recent hiring is concentrated in 2025 (49 hires) and 2026 (21 hires)—totalling only 70 external hires against 208 departures.

## Recommended Actions

1. **Accelerate external recruitment immediately** across all departments, particularly Supply Chain, Legal, and Finance (your largest teams at 128, 122, and 121 respectively) to close the 138-person gap and support growth targets.

2. **Conduct stay interviews with 2020-2023 hire cohorts** who show consistent 12-19 annual terminations; identify retention barriers before losing more mid-tenure talent.

3. **Review compensation competitiveness** (current avg: $116,202) against market benchmarks, especially for departments experiencing highest turnover.

4. **Strengthen onboarding and early-tenure engagement** for your 70 recent hires to protect this investment and improve first-year retention rates.

**Direct Answer:**
Your workforce of 1,292 people spans 12 departments with notable FTE-to-headcount gaps (Supply Chain shows 149 FTE from 128 people, a 16% surplus; Legal 146 FTE from 122 headcount), while 91% are full-time and 37% have 10+ years tenure—suggesting heavy reliance on overtime/contractors in some areas and strong retention overall.

**What Stands Out:**

| Department | Headcount | FTE | FTE/HC Ratio |
|------------|-----------|-----|--------------|
| Supply Chain | 128 | 149 | 1.16 |
| Legal | 122 | 146 | 1.20 |
| Finance | 121 | 134 | 1.11 |
| Customer Service | 90 | 100 | 1.11 |
| HR | 102 | 118 | 1.16 |

Legal, Supply Chain, Finance, and HR show 11–20% FTE inflation above headcount, signaling overtime, contractors, or temporary coverage. Only 9% part-time staff (121 of 1,292) yet FTE exceeds headcount in half your departments. Tenure is healthy (36% have 10+ years, 34% have 5–10 years) but only 19 people joined in the past year—recruitment appears slow.

**Recommended Actions:**

1. **Audit Legal and Supply Chain workload:** Investigate why 20% and 16% FTE premiums exist. Consider converting high-overtime roles or contractor positions into permanent hires to reduce cost and burnout risk.

2. **Accelerate hiring for understaffed functions:** With only 19 new hires (<1 year tenure) across 1,292 staff, ramp up recruitment in departments showing FTE strain to normalize ratios toward 1.0.

3. **Expand flexible work options:** Leverage your tenured workforce (70% with 5+ years) by piloting part-time or job-share models in high-FTE departments to distribute workload sustainably.

4. **Balance divisional distribution:** Divisions range 248–273 headcount; ensure resourcing aligns with strategic priorities and workload, not historical inertia.

## Diversity & Inclusion Analysis

**What stands out:** Your workforce shows reasonable gender balance overall (~44% female company-wide), but notable imbalances exist in specific departments, and female representation drops sharply at mid-career pay grades. Generationally, Millennials dominate (555, 43% of workforce), while Gen Z is emerging (241, 19%).

### Gender Balance by Department

| Department | Female | Male | Non-binary | % Female |
|------------|--------|------|------------|----------|
| Procurement | 62 | 49 | 7 | 53% |
| Legal | 46 | 71 | 5 | 38% |
| IT | 37 | 50 | 7 | 39% |
| Operations | 39 | 51 | 4 | 41% |
| Supply Chain | 52 | 69 | 7 | 41% |

**Why this matters:** Legal, IT, Operations and Supply Chain skew male (38-41% female), while female representation at pay grades 2 and 4 drops to 39%, suggesting mid-career advancement barriers. Non-binary representation is minimal (4% overall) but present across most departments.

### Generational Distribution
- **Millennials**: 555 (43%)
- **Gen X**: 359 (28%)
- **Gen Z**: 241 (19%)
- **Baby Boomers**: 137 (11%)

### Recommended Actions

1. **Address mid-career equity gaps**: Investigate why female representation falls at pay grades 2 (39%) and 4 (39%). Review promotion criteria, sponsorship access, and flexible work policies affecting caregiving years.

2. **Target recruitment in under-represented areas**: Partner with IT, Legal, and Operations leaders to diversify talent pipelines and review job descriptions for gendered language.

3. **Prepare for generational transition**: With 137 Baby Boomers nearing retirement, formalize knowledge transfer and ensure Gen Z (241) receives mentoring and development.

4. **Strengthen non-binary inclusion**: Review systems, policies, and manager training to support the 64 non-binary employees equitably.

## Compensation & Pay Grade Analysis

**What stands out:** Compensation is well-controlled across pay grades with compa-ratios clustering tightly around 1.0 (range 0.994–1.014), indicating consistent pay-to-midpoint alignment. However, **Non-binary employees earn significantly less overall** (avg. $105,149) compared to Male ($116,907) and Female ($116,630) colleagues—a gap of approximately $11,500–$11,800.

### Department Salary Comparison

| Department | Avg Salary | Employee Count |
|---|---:|---:|
| Marketing | $121,068 | 102 |
| Operations | $120,465 | 94 |
| R&D | $118,866 | 104 |
| Legal | $110,987 | 122 |
| Sales | $112,838 | 103 |

Department variation is modest (±5% around the enterprise mean), suggesting balanced grade distribution rather than systematic pay inequity by function.

### Gender Pay by Grade

The Non-binary gap persists inconsistently: at grade 1 they earn less ($53,239 vs. ~$54,400), but at grades 3, 5, 6, and 7 they earn *more* than both Male and Female peers. Small sample sizes (2–14 per grade) make these swings volatile, but the overall average deficit warrants attention.

**Recommended Actions:**

1. **Conduct a pay-equity audit** for Non-binary employees, controlling for tenure, performance ratings, and role. The $11,500 gap may reflect grade/tenure mix rather than bias, but verify with regression analysis.
2. **Review promotion velocity** by gender identity across grades 1–4 to ensure Non-binary talent progresses at comparable rates.
3. **Stabilize grade distributions** in Legal and Sales (lowest avg. salaries) to confirm they aren't under-graded relative to role complexity.
4. **Celebrate strong compa-ratio discipline** (0.99–1.01) while monitoring grade 3 (1.014) and grade 8 (1.012) for budget sustainability.

The 2025 performance ratings show a **healthy right-skew distribution** with 529 employees (41%) rated Exceeds or Exceptional, while only 251 (19%) fall below expectations. However, **department performance varies significantly**, and the 237 high-potential employees represent just 18% of the reviewed workforce.

## Department Performance Overview

| Department | Avg Rating | High Potentials | Reviews |
|------------|-----------|----------------|---------|
| Legal | 3.41 | 29 | 122 |
| Sales | 3.39 | 30 | 103 |
| IT | 3.09 | 15 | 94 |
| Human Resources | 3.21 | 24 | 102 |

Legal and Sales lead (3.41, 3.39), while IT trails at 3.09 with the fewest high-potentials (15 from 94 reviews, 16%). This IT gap is concerning given the strategic importance of technology capabilities.

## Recommended Actions

1. **IT talent intervention**: Conduct stay interviews with IT's 15 high-potentials and assess whether workload, tooling, or leadership gaps explain the lower ratings. Consider targeted skill development and competitive benchmarking.

2. **Calibrate the 33 Unsatisfactory ratings**: Ensure performance improvement plans are in place with clear 90-day milestones, coaching support, and fair documentation before any exit decisions.

3. **Accelerate high-potential development**: With only 237 (18%) identified as high-potential, design rotational assignments and mentorship pairs between top performers in Legal/Sales and emerging talent in underperforming departments.

4. **Balance potential vs. performance**: Review the 377 "Low potential" employees—some may be solid, steady contributors. Ensure potential assessments reflect growth capacity, not just current role fit, to avoid demotivating reliable performers.

## Learning Engagement Analysis

**Key Finding:** We have strong enrollment (3,201 total) with 60.6% completed, but 965 learners (30.1%) are stuck in progress and completion rates vary significantly by department—Marketing lags at 53.2% while Finance leads at 64.9%.

### What Stands Out

| Metric | Finding |
|--------|---------|
| **Overall Status** | 1,941 completed (60.6%), 965 in progress (30.1%), 295 not started (9.2%) |
| **Category Focus** | Professional skills dominate (1,123 enrollments, 6,604 hours); Data & Analytics trails (252 enrollments, 1,486 hours) |
| **Top Courses** | Advanced Excel highest completion (66.1%); Cloud Fundamentals lowest (55.2%) despite 281 enrollments |
| **Department Gap** | 11.7 percentage-point spread between Finance (64.9%) and Marketing (53.2%) |

**Why This Matters:** The 965 "In Progress" enrollments represent stalled development and potential disengagement. Marketing's lower completion (53.2%) and IT's modest learning hours (1,230) despite technical needs suggest capacity or prioritization issues. Cloud Fundamentals' low completion (55.2%) may signal content or relevance problems.

### Recommended Actions

1. **Launch a completion campaign** targeting the 965 in-progress learners: send manager nudges, offer dedicated "learning hours," and investigate drop-off points in Cloud Fundamentals and Effective Communication.

2. **Partner with Marketing and IT leadership** to understand completion barriers—consider lighter-touch micro-learning formats or adjusting workload expectations during learning periods.

3. **Expand Data & Analytics offerings** (currently only 252 enrollments) given workforce analytics priorities; pilot role-specific learning paths.

4. **Recognize Finance, Engineering, and Procurement** (all >63% completion) as learning culture exemplars and share their enablement practices company-wide.
recruiting:
**Recruiting health is mixed: 80 positions filled and 62 still open out of 160 total requisitions, but our 71-day average time-to-fill and very narrow funnel (23% of applicants interviewed, only 8% of interviews converted to offers) signal process bottlenecks.**

## What stands out

| Metric | Value | Issue |
|--------|-------|-------|
| Avg time-to-fill | 71 days | Long cycle |
| Application→Interview | 23% (1,012/4,458) | Screening bottleneck |
| Interview→Offer | 8% (80/1,012) | Low conversion |
| Sales time-to-fill | 85 days | Slowest department |
| Operations time-to-fill | 76 days | Second-slowest |

**By department:** Sales (85 days), HR (84 days), Operations (76 days) and R&D (75 days) lag significantly behind Engineering (59 days) and Procurement (60 days). Customer Service has strong applicant flow (559 applications, 6 open reqs) but still takes 74 days to fill.

## Recommended actions

1. **Accelerate screening in high-volume departments** – Finance (445 applications) and Legal (455 applications) attract strong interest; pilot AI-assisted résumé screening or structured phone screens to move qualified candidates to interview faster.

2. **Diagnose Sales and HR bottlenecks** – Interview hiring managers in these departments (85 and 84 days respectively) to identify approval delays, unclear requirements, or insufficient interview capacity, then assign dedicated recruiting support.

3. **Improve interview-to-offer conversion** – An 8% rate suggests misalignment between screening and role fit or delayed decision-making. Implement structured scorecards and commit to offer decisions within 5 business days of final interviews.

4. **Benchmark Engineering's process** – At 59 days and strong outcomes, replicate their intake and feedback practices across slower departments.

**New-hire onboarding is at serious risk across all three companies due to a global laptop shortage** *(demo enrichment data)*. Both standard (LAP-STD-14) and engineering laptops (LAP-ENG-16) are backordered, with lead times blown out from 5–7 days to **42 days**—an OEM memory/CPU allocation shortage affecting preferred IT resellers in US Operations, EU Operations, and Japan Operations.

## Current Inventory vs. Demand

| Company | Site | Item | On-Hand | Already Reserved | Available for New Hires |
|---------|------|------|---------|------------------|------------------------|
| US Operations | Palo Alto IT Depot | LAP-STD-14 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| US Operations | Palo Alto IT Depot | LAP-ENG-16 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| EU Operations | Walldorf IT Depot | LAP-STD-14 | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| EU Operations | Walldorf IT Depot | LAP-ENG-16 | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| Japan Operations | Tokyo IT Depot | LAP-STD-14 | 3 | 3 | 0 |

**Every kit requires 2 critical items**, and laptops are among them. With zero uncommitted stock and a 42-day wait, any new hire starting in the next six weeks will face day-one delays.

## Recommended Actions

1. **Qualify alternative suppliers immediately** for equivalent-spec laptops to break the single-source dependency and restore a <10-day lead time.
2. **Prioritize incoming hires by criticality**: reserve the next delivery batch for engineering roles (higher item count) and revenue-critical positions.
3. **Communicate proactively** with hiring managers and candidates about potential equipment delays; offer loaner/refurbished units or staggered start dates where feasible.
4. **Establish a safety-stock policy** (e.g., 10-unit buffer per site per critical SKU) to absorb future supply shocks.

Your organization has **more managers (668) than individual contributors (624)**, an inverted structure that typically indicates over-layering and can slow decision-making and increase costs.

**Spans of control and critical positions by department:**

| Department | Avg Span | Critical Positions |
|------------|----------|-------------------|
| R&D | 7.7 | 18 |
| Operations | 7.2 | 14 |
| Finance | 7.2 | 18 |
| Engineering | 6.8 | 20 |
| Supply Chain | 6.3 | 22 |
| Customer Service | 6.2 | 14 |
| Legal | 6.2 | 19 |

Average spans range from 6.2 to 7.7—relatively narrow across all departments. While ideal spans vary by complexity, spans below 5-6 often signal excess management layers. Supply Chain stands out with 22 critical positions yet only a 6.3 average span, suggesting potential succession risk if those key roles lack backup.

Your largest divisions are Division 3 US Operations (109 headcount), Division 1 EU Operations (101), and Division 4 EU Operations (93).

**Recommended actions:**

1. **Audit management layers:** Map reporting levels from CEO to frontline in each department. Target consolidation where managers supervise fewer than 5 people and work is routine.

2. **Widen spans selectively:** Pilot increasing spans to 8-10 in R&D, Operations and Finance where current averages are highest, redistributing management capacity or converting roles to senior IC positions.

3. **Succession-plan critical roles:** Prioritize Supply Chain (22), Engineering (20) and Legal (19). Identify successors and cross-training plans for each critical position.

4. **Rebalance manager/IC ratio:** Aim for 1:2 or better. Assess whether all 668 management roles require direct reports or if some should transition to expert/lead IC tracks.

The roster comprises **1,292 active employees and 208 terminated**, with remarkably balanced distribution across 14 job titles and stable, healthy tenure (7–8 years average across most roles). The top 15 earners are all VPs at pay grade 8, spanning every major function—Sales, R&D, Operations, Customer Service, HR, Marketing, Finance, IT, Engineering, and Supply Chain—with salaries clustering tightly between $199,781 and $211,683.

| Job Title | Count | Avg Salary | Avg Tenure (yrs) |
|-----------|-------|------------|------------------|
| VP | 98 | $181,781 | 7.5 |
| Director | 78 | $164,738 | 7.6 |
| Principal | 75 | $163,275 | 7.4 |
| Senior Manager | 107 | $145,076 | 6.4 |
| Lead | 91 | $127,740 | 7.7 |
| Associate | 90 | $54,391 | 8.0 |

**What stands out:**  
1. **Strong retention and experience depth** – tenure averaging 7+ years signals stability and institutional knowledge.  
2. **Concentrated top compensation** – all 15 highest earners are VPs; the narrowest VP tenure is just 1 year (E100961, Supply Chain), raising questions about external hires vs. internal promotion equity.  
3. **Healthy title distribution** – no single level dominates, suggesting career pathways exist, though Senior Managers (107) outnumber Directors (78).

**Recommended actions:**

1. **Map promotion velocity** for Senior Managers and Principals into Director/VP roles; if external VP hires consistently outpace internal promotions, design accelerated leadership programs to retain high-performers.  
2. **Conduct pay-equity audits** within each title band, especially for Senior Managers (avg. $145k) and Leads (avg. $128k), to ensure gender, tenure, and location equity.  
3. **Profile the 208 terminated employees** by exit reason, department, and tenure to identify retention hot spots.  
4. **Benchmark Associate salaries** ($54k avg.) against market to safeguard early-career attraction and diversity pipelines.
